document_text:
Verdo Foods - Company and Product Brief

Launch of Proteo Crisps in France. Internal document, prepared for the launch planning team. All

companies, people and figures in this document are fictional and used for demonstration only.

1. Company overview

Verdo Foods S.r.l. is an Italian food company founded in 2020 in Bologna by Giulia Ferri, a food

technologist, and Marco Bassi, former category manager at a large Italian retailer. The company

develops  savoury  snacks  made  from  legumes,  with  a  focus  on  high  protein  content,  short

ingredient lists and sustainable packaging.

In  2024  Verdo  Foods  had  28  employees  and  a  turnover  of  4.2  million  euros,  almost  entirely  in

Italy. Its products are sold in about 2,300 points of sale in Italy (supermarkets, organic shops and

a  selection  of  gyms)  and  through  its  own  online  shop,  which  accounts  for  9%  of  sales.  The

company closed its first profitable year in 2024 and raised a second funding round in early 2025

to finance its first international launch.

Mission: make plant-based protein an everyday snack, not a niche product for athletes or vegans.

2. The product: Proteo Crisps

Proteo  Crisps  are  oven-baked  crisps  made  from  chickpea  flour  and  pea  protein.  They  were

launched in Italy in 2022 and are now the company's best-selling line, with 61% of its turnover.

-    15  g  of  protein  per  40  g  bag,  about  30%  more  than  the  leading  plant-based  protein  crisps  in

Italy.

-    Three  flavours:  Sea  Salt,  Rosemary,  and  Smoked  Paprika.  A  fourth  flavour  (Herbes  de

Provence) is being developed specifically for France.

-  Only six ingredients, no palm oil, no additives; vegan and gluten-free certified.

-  Nutri-Score A for Sea Salt and Rosemary, B for Smoked Paprika.

-  Compostable packaging, introduced in 2024.

-  Shelf life of 9 months, which allows distribution through standard supermarket logistics.

In  Italian  blind  taste  tests  run  by  the  company  in  2024  (420  participants),  Proteo  Crisps  were

preferred to the leading conventional potato crisps by 47% of participants, a tie for 21%, and less

preferred by 32%. Texture was the most appreciated attribute; the Smoked Paprika flavour was

judged too strong by a quarter of participants.

3. Why France, and launch goals

France is the second largest savoury snack market in Europe and the fastest growing market for

protein  snacks  in  Southern  Europe.  French  consumers  are  familiar  with  Nutri-Score,  which  was

created  in  France,  and  the  company  sees  its  Nutri-Score  A  rating  as  a  strong  argument  on  the

shelf.

Goals for the French launch, approved by the board in June 2025:

-  Reach a 2% value share of the French protein snack category within 24 months of launch.

 -  Be listed in at least 1,500 points of sale in the first year.

-  Generate 25% of company turnover from France by the end of 2027.

-  Reach break-even on the French operation in the third year.

The launch is planned for March 2026, starting with the Paris, Lyon and Lille regions.

4. Market context

The figures below come from the NutriMarket Insights report 'Protein snacks in France 2025' and

from the France Snack Panel 2024 consumer survey (both fictional sources for this demo).

In  short,  the  protein  snack  category  is  worth  480  million  euros  and  grows  by  11%  per  year;

plant-based products are 18% of it, and 27% of French adults bought a protein snack in the last

three months.

Supermarkets  and  hypermarkets  account  for  68%  of  protein  snack  sales  in  France,  specialised

sport  and  organic  shops  for  17%,  online  for  9%,  and  gyms  and  vending  for  6%  (NutriMarket

Insights 2025).

5. Consumer groups

The  France  Snack  Panel  2024  measured  purchase  intent  for  a  high-protein,  plant-based  crisp

after showing a product concept similar to Proteo Crisps. Group sizes refer to adults aged 18 to

The founders' first instinct is to target vegans, because they show by far the highest enthusiasm

 for the concept and are the most active group on social media. The team has not yet decided on

the target group.

6. Competitive landscape

The main competitors identified by the team in France are:

-  Barebells: protein bars and snacks, strong presence in gyms and supermarkets, sport-oriented

image.

-    Gerble:  French  brand  of  health  and  wellness  foods,  widely  available  in  supermarkets,  with

some protein products.

-  Supermarket private labels, which entered the protein snack category in 2023 with lower prices.

The team has not yet carried out a detailed price comparison of competitors in France.

7. Production and distribution

Proteo Crisps are produced in the company's plant near Bologna, which currently runs at 55% of

its capacity and can supply the French launch without new investment. For France, Verdo Foods

plans  to  work  with  a  national  food  distributor  for  supermarkets  and  to  sell  directly  to  gyms  and

organic  shops  in  the  launch  regions.  The  online  shop  will  be  translated  and  will  ship  to  France

from launch day.

Packaging  will  be  adapted  to  French  labelling  rules,  with  Nutri-Score  shown  on  the  front  of  the

pack.

8. Open points

-  Choice of the target group and of the positioning for France.

-  Launch campaign concept and channel plan.

-  Name of the national distributor (negotiations ongoing with two candidates).

analysis.market_overview: The French protein snack category was worth 480M euros in 2024 and grew 11% per year from 2021 to 2024; plant-based products are 18% of it, and 27% of French adults bought a protein snack in the last three months [S2]. It sits inside a 2.9 billion euro savoury snack market [S2]. Supermarkets and hypermarkets make up 68% of protein snack sales, specialised sport and organic shops 17%, online 9%, and gyms and vending 6% [S2]. The company describes France as the second largest savoury snack market in Europe and says French shoppers know Nutri-Score [S1]. Trade press reports that protein-enriched products on shelves grew 86% between 2021 and 2025 [S12]. Private labels are 35.7% of food sales value and are priced 30-35% below equivalent national brands on average [S11]. That is a general food figure, not specific to protein snacks. All French category and segment figures come from the company document alone. No independent web source confirms them.

competitors.name: Barebells
competitors.positioning: Protein bars and snacks with a sport-oriented image, strong in gyms and supermarkets [S4]. Carrefour France promotes the bars as an in-store exclusivity [S7]. It launched five new flavours, including vegan options, in 2025 [S13]. It is a bar, not a crisp, so it competes for the same protein snack budget rather than the same product form.

competitors.name: Gerblé
competitors.positioning: French health and wellness food brand, widely available in supermarkets, with some protein products [S4]. Its almond sport and nutrition bar has 7.9 g protein and 57 g sugars per 100 g [S8]. The protein claim is therefore weak, and no Gerblé protein crisps were found.

competitors.name: Supermarket private labels
competitors.positioning: Retailer own brands that entered the protein snack category in 2023 at lower prices [S4]. Private labels on average cost 30-35% less than equivalent national brands across food [S11]. Carrefour has an own-brand protein bar (4 x 32 g) [S16]. No private-label protein crisp was found.

competitors.name: Pea Pops
competitors.positioning: Puffed (not fried) chickpea, soy, tapioca and rice crisps with 20% protein, sold through Comptoir Irlandais. They are a direct legume-crisp alternative.

competitors.name: Le Nature chickpea crisps
competitors.positioning: Organic, gluten-free chickpea crisps with sea salt. They are a source of fibre and protein, with 60% less fat and no palm oil, and are pitched at aperitif and snack occasions.

customer_needs: High-protein snacks: 27% of French adults bought a protein snack in the last three months [S2]
Plant-based protein options: plant-based products are 18% of protein snack sales and the category grows 11% per year [S2]
Healthy-looking labels that are easy to read on the shelf: French consumers are familiar with Nutri-Score [S1]
Simple ingredient lists and organic certifications, which drive European demand including France [S13]
Low sugar and good value per kilo: a French review rates protein crisps on more than 20 g protein per 100 g, under 10 g sugars and under 25 euros/kg [S9]
Lower prices in supermarkets: private labels are priced 30-35% below national brands and are growing in protein snacks [S4][S11]
Snacking as a growing eating habit, with protein-enriched products expanding on shelves [S12]

segments.label: Vegans and strict vegetarians
segments.description: Adults who follow a vegan or strict vegetarian diet. They have the highest purchase intent for a high-protein, plant-based crisp (72%) but are the smallest group [S3]. The founders lean towards them because they are the most active on social media [S3].
needs: Vegan certification and short ingredient list

segments.label: Weekly sport practitioners
segments.description: Adults who practise sport weekly. They are the largest group, with 41% purchase intent [S3]. Gyms and vending are only 6% of protein snack sales, and supermarkets 68% [S2].
needs: Convenient snack available in supermarkets and gyms

segments.label: Health-conscious office workers
segments.description: Adults at work who are attentive to health. 38% purchase intent [S3]. They overlap with the sport group [S3].
needs: Healthy snack with a clear nutrition signal such as Nutri-Score

segments.label: Parents of school-age children
segments.description: Parents of school-age children. They show the lowest purchase intent of the four groups, 22% [S3].
needs: Healthier snack option for the household

data_quality_notes: The French market figures (480M euros, +11% per year, 18% plant-based, channel shares) come only from the document, citing NutriMarket Insights 2025, which the document labels fictional. No independent French web source confirms them.

The segment sizes and purchase intents come only from the France Snack Panel 2024, which the document labels fictional. The groups overlap, so sizes must not be added. Purchase intent was measured on a concept similar to Proteo Crisps, not on the product, and intent is not actual purchase.

Missing: no reliable price for Proteo Crisps or for any competitor in French supermarkets. All price_level values are therefore 'unknown' except private labels, which the document says entered at lower prices [S4].

Barebells prices found are from non-supermarket online retailers (Primor, about 2.25-2.29 euros per 55 g bar [S5]; Idealo, a 12-bar pack from 26.16 euros, about 2.18 per bar [S6]). The Idealo page date (November 2026) is odd compared with the document timeline, so treat both as indicative only. The Carrefour post [S7] gives no price.
No Gerblé shelf price or protein crisp was found. Gerblé's protein positioning looks weak: its almond bar has 7.9 g protein and 57 g sugars per 100 g [S8].

The only crisp price benchmark is a blog range of 15-40 euros/kg [S9], a weak source. Its claim that protein crisps filled French shelves in 2026 with Doritos protéinés could not be verified for France. Doritos Protein sources describe a US launch [S10]. Doritos is therefore not listed as a competitor.
Pea Pops and Le Nature appear in the search results as legume crisps, but no price, share or distribution data was found for them. Their positioning comes from product-page snippets only.

The Mordor Intelligence page [S13] is a paid-report marketing page. Its Europe-wide statements on organic certification, simple ingredient lists and Barebells flavours are weak evidence and are not specific to France.
The private-label data [S11] cover all food, not protein snacks. No private-label protein crisp was found, only a Carrefour protein bar [S16].
The LSA 86% figure [S12] is a trade-press citation of ProtéinesXTC and covers protein-enriched products in general, not protein snacks.

Segment needs are my reading of the segments and of the document's product points (for example vegan certification, Nutri-Score). The panel does not state them directly. No independent source describes the four consumer groups.

The Italian blind taste test (420 participants, own test) is not used as a French customer need. The Smoked Paprika flavour was judged too strong by a quarter of participants, which may matter for French acceptance but is untested in France.

sources.reference: Company document, section 3 (Why France, and launch goals)

strategy.target_description: Adults aged 18-64 who practise sport weekly in France and buy protein snacks. They look for a high-protein snack they can find in the supermarket where they shop, and also in gyms and sport shops. Vegans and health-conscious office workers who also play sport are reached as a secondary audience through the same product.
strategy.positioning_statement: For active French adults who want protein in their snacks, Proteo Crisps is the savoury protein crisp: 15 g of protein per 40 g bag in a crunchy, oven-baked crisp with only six ingredients, no palm oil and no additives, and Nutri-Score A (Sea Salt, Rosemary). It is the salty alternative to the protein bar from Barebells, and it is a cleaner, higher-protein choice than supermarket private labels and Gerblé, whose protein claim is weak [S8].
strategy.value_proposition: A savoury, crunchy 15 g protein snack that fits a sporty routine. It has a short, clean label that is easy to read on the shelf (six ingredients, Nutri-Score A on two flavours, vegan and gluten-free certified), and it is a salty option instead of another sweet protein bar.
strategy.pricing_direction: Competitor prices are largely unknown: no shelf price was found for Gerblé, private labels, Pea Pops or Le Nature, and the only Barebells prices come from online retailers and are indicative (about 2.2 euros per 55 g bar [S5][S6]). Recommendation: do not compete with private labels on price. They are low-priced and run 30-35% below national brands across food [S11], so a price war would hurt a 15 g protein product with a clean label. Position at a premium to private labels and close to Barebells per serving. Stay inside the 15-40 euros/kg range of the weak crisp benchmark [S9], and test a level under the 25 euros/kg value threshold from the same review. Before fixing the price, run a shelf-price audit of Barebells, private labels, Pea Pops and Le Nature in the target supermarkets and sport shops, and check it against Verdo's costs and the break-even goal.
strategy.rationale: SEG2 is the best fit with the goals in the brief. Size and interest together: it is the largest segment, 17.5M adults (34% of adults aged 18-64), with 41% purchase intent [S3]. SEG1 has the highest intent (72%) but is only 1.3M adults (2.5%) [S3]. Even if every person in it bought, it is too small to deliver a 2% category share and 1,500 points of sale, so it cannot carry the volume goals alone. SEG3 is 9.0M with 38% intent and SEG4 is 7.1M with 22% [S3]. SEG2 is therefore about twice the size of SEG3 with higher intent, and it overlaps with SEG3, so a sport-led launch also reaches part of the office-worker group. Sizes must not be added because the groups overlap, and intent was measured on a similar concept, not on the product [S3]. Accessibility: supermarkets and hypermarkets are 68% of protein snack sales and sport and organic shops 17% [S2], so supermarket reach through the national distributor is needed for the 1,500-point goal. Gyms and vending are only 6% [S2], so gyms support credibility but cannot carry volume. This is consistent with Verdo's plan of a distributor plus direct sales to gyms and organic shops (the distributor is not yet chosen). Competition: Barebells is strong in gyms and supermarkets [S4], but it is a bar, not a crisp. No Gerblé protein crisp and no private-label protein crisp were found [S4][S8][S16]. The direct legume-crisp alternatives, Pea Pops (20% protein) [S14] and Le Nature [S15], have no known price or distribution data. Category: protein snacks are worth 480M euros and grow 11% a year, and 27% of adults bought one in the last three months [S2]. For reference, a 2% share is about 9.6M euros at 2024 category size (my calculation); this is a company-document figure with no independent confirmation. Claims used: protein per bag, six ingredients, no palm oil, certifications and Nutri-Score, which French shoppers know [S1]. Claims not used: the "30% more protein" comparison, because it was measured against the leading Italian plant-based crisp and is not valid in France, and the Italian taste test (47% preferred), because it was not run in France. Smoked Paprika was judged too strong by a quarter of Italian testers, so lead with Sea Salt and Rosemary (Nutri-Score A) and test Smoked Paprika in France. Vegans (SEG1) are served as a secondary audience on Instagram and in organic shops, since the founders see them as the most active on social media [S3]; this is an assumption about reach, not evidence of sales. Risks: all French market and segment data come from one document labelled fictional, with no independent confirmation; protein-enriched shelf growth [S12] is general, not specific to snacks; price and marketing budget are not set.

campaign.concept: Sweet is the default for protein snacks; Proteo Crisps flips it. The campaign, "Côté salé", puts the savoury crunch at the centre of the sporty routine: after the session, on the way home, in the gym bag. Every piece shows the same proof points: 15 g of protein per 40 g bag, six ingredients, no palm oil, no additives, and Nutri-Score A on Sea Salt and Rosemary. This expresses the positioning of the savoury protein crisp for active adults.

key_messages.body: 15 g de protéines, 6 ingrédients, 0 huile de palme, 0 additif. Proteo Crisps, croustillante et cuite au four. Végane, sans gluten. Votre sac de sport a trouvé son nouveau réflexe. #CôtéSalé

content_ideas: In-store tasting stands and branded shelf-strip displays in French supermarkets and hypermarkets during launch month, placed next to the protein snack section, with the 15 g / 6 ingredients / Nutri-Score A message
Shelf-edge and end-of-aisle displays in supermarkets showing the two Nutri-Score A flavours (Sea Salt, Rosemary) first, with a simple 'Côté salé' header
Gym poster and counter display kit with sample bags for partner gyms and sport shops, with a QR code linking to the online shop
Instagram Reels series 'Côté salé': short post-workout and gym-bag moments featuring the crunch, ending on the 15 g per 40 g bag proof point
Instagram carousel explaining the label in six ingredients, one slide per ingredient, plus the certifications (vegan, gluten-free) and compostable packaging
Organic shop shelf talkers and tasting days highlighting the short ingredient list, no palm oil, no additives and vegan and gluten-free certifications
Online shop discovery box with the three flavours and a launch landing page built around the 'Côté salé' idea
Collaboration with French amateur sport and fitness creators on Instagram, who share a snack routine with Proteo Crisps (claims limited to the approved product facts)
campaign.visual_direction: Clean, energetic and appetising, with a savoury rather than 'sweet fitness' feel. Palette: warm chickpea beige and off-white as the base, with bold accent colours per flavour (sea blue for Sea Salt, herb green for Rosemary, deep red for Smoked Paprika) and a strong dark charcoal for typography. Photography: close-up macro shots of the crisp's crunch, natural daylight, real everyday sport moments (gym bag, locker room, park run, commute) with diverse adults aged 18-64, no body-transformation imagery. Graphic device: a bold '15 g' badge and a six-dot ingredient icon repeated on all materials, plus the Nutri-Score A logo only on Sea Salt and Rosemary. Packaging cues: matte, paper-like compostable bag with large flavour name, simple typography, visible 'Côté salé' flash, vegan and gluten-free marks, and the ingredient count on the front. Text is in French, short and factual.

issues.message: This need rests on S13, a paid-report marketing page. It covers Europe, not France, and the notes admit it is weak evidence. The price and sugar thresholds in the next need rest on a single blog (S9). Neither need is backed by a French consumer source. Mark them as hypotheses, or drop them or replace them with a French source. Do not present them as established needs of French buyers. Evidence: analysis.customer_needs = "Simple ingredient lists and organic certifications, which drive European demand including France [S13]"

S4 only says private labels entered the protein snack category in 2023 at lower prices. S11 is a general food comparison. Neither source supports the claim that they are 'growing in protein snacks'. Remove the growth claim, or cite a source for it. Evidence: analysis.customer_needs = "private labels are priced 30-35% below national brands and are growing in protein snacks [S4][S11]"

The analysis has no protein figure for private labels. It found only a Carrefour protein bar and no private-label crisp, and it gives no protein figure for that bar. The only Gerblé evidence is one almond bar at 7.9 g per 100 g. The comparison with private labels therefore has no supporting input, and the Gerblé comparison rests on a bar, not a crisp. Reword the statement to say what is documented, such as 15 g per 40 g bag and a six-ingredient label. Alternatively, add a like-for-like protein comparison of French products before making the claim. Evidence: strategy.positioning_statement = "it is a cleaner, higher-protein choice than supermarket private labels and Gerblé"

The differentiation is set against bars (Barebells, Gerblé), which are a different product form. The analysis lists two direct legume-crisp competitors: Pea Pops (20% protein, chickpea) and Le Nature (chickpea, no palm oil, organic, gluten-free). The value proposition does not say how Proteo differs from them. Six ingredients, no palm oil and gluten-free are already offered by Le Nature. Add a clear point of difference against these two, for example the protein density, which is higher than Pea Pops if you compare per 100 g. Do this before launch. Evidence: strategy.value_proposition = "it is a salty option instead of another sweet protein bar"

The company document plans direct sales to gyms and organic shops, plus a distributor for supermarkets. It does not plan to sell in sport shops. Instagram is a communication channel, not a sales channel, and it is mainly justified by the vegan secondary audience, not by the sport-practitioner target. Clarify the sales channels against the document's plan. Say what Instagram is meant to do for SEG2. Evidence: strategy.channels = "Gyms and sport shops"

This supermarket message is about a clean label and nothing else. It has no protein-per-serving hook and no sport or active-routine angle. The target is weekly sport practitioners, whose needs are high protein and convenience, so it speaks more to health-conscious shoppers. It also names only two ingredients next to the headline "Six ingrédients", which is confusing. Add the 15 g protein and sport cue, and either list all six ingredients or reword the line. Evidence: campaign.key_messages[1].body = "Pois chiche, protéines de pois et c'est tout ce qu'il faut à lire."

The two supermarket/hypermarket messages repeat the same proof points (15 g, six ingredients, no palm oil, no additives). The sport and gym-bag angle is missing from both, although it is the core of the concept. Give the second supermarket message a different job, for example an on-shelf sport moment or the Côté salé versus sweet bars idea, instead of a second list of label facts. Evidence: campaign.key_messages[0].body = "Retrouvez-la au rayon snacking protéiné."
